summary: "Luke lists Jesus in Jacob's family. But Genesis promises a multitude—does one descendant fulfil it?"
ot_reference: "Gen 28:14"
ot_text: "Your descendants will be like the dust of the earth, and you will spread out to the west and east and north and south. All the families of the earth will be blessed through you and your offspring."
ot_note: ""
christian_case: "Genesis carries Abraham's worldwide promise forward through Jacob: a great family will spread in every direction, and all families will be blessed through Jacob and his offspring. Luke explicitly places Jesus in the line Jacob–Isaac–Abraham, then extends his genealogy to Adam, fitting the Gospel's universal scope. Elsewhere the New Testament centres the Abrahamic blessing in Christ. Christians can therefore present Jesus as Israel's representative descendant through whom the family promise reaches the nations. His place in the ancestral line is an explicit part of Luke's story."
critical_case: "Genesis immediately describes Jacob's offspring as numerous as the dust and spreading across the land. It is promising a people, not uniquely identifying one descendant. Luke asserts that Jesus belongs to this line but provides genealogy rather than a citation or interpretation of Genesis 28:14. That ancestry criterion is shared across Israel, so it cannot distinguish Jesus by itself. Connecting worldwide blessing specifically with him depends on the later representative-Christ argument, not on genealogy alone."
verdict_label: "Explicit ancestry; insufficiently specific prophecy"
verdict: "Luke explicitly presents Jesus as Jacob's descendant, so the modest ancestry claim works within the Gospel. Christian theology can also view him as the representative heir through whom the blessing reaches the nations. Genesis itself promises a multitude rather than uniquely identifying him: covenantal fulfilment is stronger here than predictive evidence."
